svg.aria-label: Diagram: why a JDBC connection URL is closer to code than to configuration. On the left, how a connection string is usually handled: it is stored in a properties file, an environment variable, a Secrets Manager secret or an infrastructure-as-code template, and it is reviewed as though the worst case were pointing at the wrong database. In the centre, what the Amazon Redshift JDBC driver version 2 documentation says connection URL parameters can actually instruct the driver to do, all of them settable in the URL and none of them case sensitive. Plugin_Name takes the fully qualified class name of a credentials provider plugin, so the URL names a class the driver loads. socketFactory specifies a socket factory for socket creation and SSLFactory specifies the SSL factory used when connecting without a server certificate, both class-name valued. IniFile gives the full path of an ini file the driver reads its configuration from and IniSection names the section within it, so the URL can redirect configuration to an arbitrary local file. LogPath gives the folder the driver writes log files to, and an invalid value sends output to standard out instead. StsEndpointUrl specifies an AWS Security Token Service endpoint and causes the Region option to be ignored, though it must be HTTPS. On the right, CVE-2026-8178: under certain conditions the driver could load and execute arbitrary classes when processing connection URL parameters, in versions earlier than 2.2.2, fixed in 2.2.2, with no published CVSS score and no workaround other than upgrading, including any forked or derivative code. A closing panel notes that the driver is a Type 4 driver, meaning pure Java inside the calling process, so class loading there executes with whatever identity that JVM holds, typically an instance or task role. A final panel records two insecure-looking documented defaults found on the same page: SSL_Insecure defaults to true so the identity provider server certificate is not verified, and SSLMode defaults to verify-ca rather than the verify-full that AWS itself recommends, which is the setting that checks the host name matches.
svg.title: A JDBC connection URL is closer to code than to configuration
svg.text: A connection string looks like config. The option list says otherwise.
Every parameter below is documented and intended. CVE-2026-8178 is that surface failing, not a new one appearing.
reviewed as though the worst case
What a URL parameter can instruct
a local file to read config from
a folder to write files to
and option names are not case sensitive
no CVSS, no workaround but upgrade
Why class loading here is not a database problem
A Type 4 driver is pure Java running inside your process — a Glue job, a Spark executor, a BI server, a Lambda.
Loading a class there executes with whatever identity that JVM holds, which on AWS is usually an instance or task role.
So the question is not “can a user pick the database”
It is: can anything outside your code contribute a fragment of that URL? A BI tool with user-defined data sources · a
multi-tenant product taking a customer endpoint · a Glue job whose options come from a parameter · a URL built from a row.
Two documented defaults on the same page, worth setting explicitly
defaults to true — “the driver doesn’t check the authenticity of the IDP server certificate”
defaults to verify-ca — AWS recommends verify-full, which also checks the host name
The recommended value is not the default value, in both cases.
Upgrading closes the class-loading path. Plugin_Name, socketFactory, SSLFactory and IniFile are features, and are still there.
Patch forked and shaded copies too — a vendored driver does not upgrade with the dependency, and does not show up as the driver.
Build URLs from a template with a fixed parameter set. Allowlist parameter names case-insensitively.
